transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Angle measure}\par Convert between degrees and radians.\par For example: express \(45^\circ\) in radians.\par \textbf{2. Length and area}\par Use a radius and an angle to find an arc length, sector perimeter or area.

\textbf{3. Trigonometric equations}\par Solve \(\sin x=\tfrac12\) for \(0\le x<\pi\).\par \textbf{4. Small angles}\par Explain why, for small \(\theta\) in radians,\[\sin5\theta+\tan2\theta-\cos2\theta\approx2\theta^2+7\theta-1.\]

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Degrees and radians}\par A degree is \(1/360\) of a full turn. One radian is the angle whose arc length equals the radius.
A full circle has arc length \(2\pi r\). How many radians is a complete turn?

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Why use radians?}\par Radians connect angle directly to length. They also give the simplest formulas in calculus.\[\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x)=\cos x\]\par This formula assumes that \(x\) is measured in radians.

\textbf{A useful distinction}\par Degrees remain convenient for everyday geometry.\par Radians are the standard angle measure in calculus and many mathematical models.\par Always check the angle unit before using a trigonometric function.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5A, Question 8}\par The curve is\[y=\cos\left(x-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right),\qquad-2\pi\le x\le2\pi.\]\par Find all intersections with the coordinate axes. (3 marks)
For the \(y\)-axis, put \(x=0\):\[y=\cos(-2\pi/3)=-\tfrac12.\]\par The intercept is \((0,-\tfrac12)\).

For the \(x\)-axis:\[x-\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac\pi2+k\pi.\]\par In the given interval the intercepts are\[\left(-\frac{11\pi}6,0\right),\left(-\frac{5\pi}6,0\right),\]\[\left(\frac\pi6,0\right),\left(\frac{7\pi}6,0\right).\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Arc length}\par An angle of 1 radian subtends an arc of length \(r\). An angle of \(\theta\) radians therefore subtends what arc length?
\[\boxed{l=r\theta}\]\par Use the same length units for \(l\) and \(r\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Sector perimeter}\par A sector has radius \(r\), angle \(\theta\) radians and perimeter \(P\). Express \(r\) in terms of \(P\) and \(\theta\).
\textbf{2. Garden pond}\par A pond is bounded by a straight chord \(AB=2.4\text{ m}\) and the major arc of a circle of radius \(2\text{ m}\). Find the curved boundary length.
Bisect the minor central angle:\[x=\sin^{-1}(1.2/2)\approx0.643501.\]\par Major angle: \(\theta=2\pi-2x\).\[l=2(2\pi-2x)\approx\boxed{9.99\text{ m}}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C2 January 2005, Q7}\par Triangle \(ABC\) has \(AB=8\text{ cm}\), \(AC=11\text{ cm}\), and \(\angle BAC=0.7\) radians.\par An arc \(BD\), centre \(A\) and radius 8 cm, meets \(AC\) at \(D\).\par Region \(R\) is bounded by \(BC\), \(CD\) and arc \(BD\).\par (a) Find arc \(BD\).\par (b) Find the perimeter of \(R\), to 3 significant figures.
\(CD=11-8=3\text{ cm}\).\par By the cosine rule:\[BC=\sqrt{8^2+11^2-2(8)(11)\cos0.7}.\]\[P=5.6+3+BC=\boxed{15.7\text{ cm}}\ (3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5C, Question 5}\par An annular sector has inner radius \(3\text{ cm}\), outer radius \(5\text{ cm}\), and angle \(\theta\) radians.\par (a) Find its perimeter when \(\theta=0.8\).\par (b) Find \(\theta\) when its perimeter is \(14\text{ cm}\).
The two arcs have lengths \(3\theta\) and \(5\theta\). Each straight edge is 2 cm.\[P=3\theta+5\theta+2+2=8\theta+4.\]\par At \(\theta=0.8\), \(P=\boxed{10.4\text{ cm}}\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5C, Question 6}\par A sector has radius \(r\text{ cm}\) and angle \(1.2\) radians. It has the same perimeter as a square of area \(36\text{ cm}^2\).\par Find \(r\).
The square has side \(\sqrt{36}=6\text{ cm}\), so perimeter 24 cm.\par The sector perimeter is\[2r+1.2r=3.2r.\]\[3.2r=24\implies\boxed{r=7.5\text{ cm}}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Sector area in degrees}\par A sector with angle \(\alpha\) degrees is a fraction \(\alpha/360\) of the circle.
\[A=\frac{180\theta/\pi}{360}\pi r^2=\boxed{\frac12r^2\theta}.\]\par The angle \(\theta\) must be in radians.

transcription.tex: \textbf{MAT 2012, Question 1J}\par Two chords \(PQ,PR\) of a unit circle meet at an angle \(\theta\) at \(P\).\par Find the largest possible area bounded by the chords and the arc \(QR\) opposite \(P\).

The arc \(QR\) subtends \(2\theta\) at the centre. Its segment area is fixed.\par Therefore maximise triangle \(PQR\): its base is fixed, and its height is greatest when \(P\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(QR\).

In this symmetric arrangement, the region comprises a sector of angle \(2\theta\) and two triangles of area \(\tfrac12\sin\theta\).\[A_{\max}=\frac12(2\theta)+2\left(\frac12\sin\theta\right)=\boxed{\theta+\sin\theta}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{1. Edexcel January 2007, Q6}\par Solve \(2\cos^2x+1=5\sin x\) for \(0\le x<2\pi\). Give exact answers.
\[2(1-\sin^2x)+1=5\sin x.\]\[(2\sin x-1)(\sin x+3)=0.\]\par Reject \(\sin x=-3\). Thus\[\boxed{x=\pi/6,\ 5\pi/6}.\]

First use \(0\le3\theta\le6\pi\).\[3\theta=\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\frac{7\pi}3,\frac{8\pi}3,\frac{13\pi}3,\frac{14\pi}3.\]\par Divide every value by 3:\[\boxed{\theta=\frac\pi9,\frac{2\pi}9,\frac{7\pi}9,\frac{8\pi}9,\frac{13\pi}9,\frac{14\pi}9}.\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Exercise 5E, Question 15 — measurements as printed}\par In triangle \(ABC\), \(AB=5\text{ cm}\), \(AC=12\text{ cm}\), \(\angle ABC=0.5\) radians, and \(\angle ACB=x\).\par (a) Find \(\sin x\), to 3 decimal places.\par (b) Find the possible triangle angle \(x\), to 2 decimal places.
By the sine rule:\[\frac{\sin x}{5}=\frac{\sin0.5}{12}.\]\[\boxed{\sin x=0.200}\ (3\text{ d.p.}).\]

\(x_1=\sin^{-1}(5\sin0.5/12)\approx0.2011\).\par The second sine solution is \(\pi-x_1\), but it exceeds \(\pi-0.5\), so it cannot be a triangle angle.\[\boxed{x=0.20\text{ rad}}.\]\par With these measurements there is only one triangle.

transcription.tex: \textbf{MAT 2010, Question 1C}\par How many solutions in \(0\le x\le2\pi\) satisfy\[\sin^2x+3\sin x\cos x+2\cos^2x=0?\]

\[(\sin x+2\cos x)(\sin x+\cos x)=0.\]\par \(\cos x=0\) is not a solution. Divide by \(\cos x\):\[\tan x=-2\quad\text{or}\quad\tan x=-1.\]\par Each has two solutions in the interval. They are distinct, so the total is \(\boxed4\).

transcription.tex: \textbf{When the angle is small}\par For \(\theta\) near zero, measured in radians:\[\boxed{\sin\theta\approx\theta,\quad\tan\theta\approx\theta}\]\[\boxed{\cos\theta\approx1-\frac{\theta^2}{2}}.\]\par These approximations improve as \(\theta\) approaches zero.

\textbf{The unit matters}\par Near zero, the graph \(y=\sin x\) is close to \(y=x\) only when \(x\) is measured in radians.\par For example, \(\sin(0.1)\approx0.0998334\), whereas \(\sin(0.1^\circ)\approx0.00174533\).

sourceMapping.method: Source-checked native text and LaTeX; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Geometric explanation}\par For a unit circle and \(0<\theta<\pi/2\):\par Inner triangle area \(=\tfrac12\sin\theta\).\par Sector area \(=\tfrac12\theta\).\par Outer tangent triangle area \(=\tfrac12\tan\theta\).\par Comparing areas gives\[\sin\theta<\theta<\tan\theta.\]

Dividing by \(\theta>0\) gives\[\cos\theta<\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}<1.\]\par Both bounds approach 1 as \(\theta\to0\). Hence\[\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\to1,\qquad\sin\theta\approx\theta.\]\par Radians are essential because the sector area used was \(\theta/2\).
